setup-account.text:
Create a Host Account (~5 minutes)
Earn by hosting your GPUs on Vast.ai. To become a host, you’ll need to convert your account to a host account and agree to our hosting agreement.
Note: Host (supplier) accounts must be separate from Client (renter) accounts. If you want to rent GPUs on Vast.ai, create separate accounts.
Recommended: Host with a Team Host Account (~1 minute)
If you want to manage hosting with your team, please create a team before accepting the host agreement.
1) Create your team account by following the official quickstart guide:
https://docs.vast.ai/guides/teams/teams-quickstart
2) Switch to the team account you created. Click your profile icon and select the team account from the menu.
3) Go to the setup page here and agree to the hosting agreement for the team account.

setup-requirements.text:
Minimum Requirements for Verification (~1 minute)
Your machine must meet all of the following to be eligible for verification.
Component
Minimum Requirement
OS
Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS minimum, 24.04 LTS recommended. Server edition only; releases above 24.04 are not supported
GPU
NVIDIA Maxwell or newer, all GPUs the same model. More than 7 GB VRAM per GPU
NVIDIA Driver
Must support CUDA 11.8 or newer. Latest stable recommended
CUDA
11.8 or newer. On ARM64, 12.6 or newer. Latest recommended
CPU
x86_64 or ARM64 with AVX support. 2 physical cores per GPU
RAM
At least 95% of total GPU VRAM (0.95 × VRAM per GPU × number of GPUs)
Storage
SSD. At least a 200 GB dedicated partition for Docker storage, and 20 GB free on the root partition
PCIe
More than 2.85 GiB/s per GPU
Network
500 Mbps download and upload. Wired Ethernet, fiber recommended
Ports
Public IPv4 address with 5 forwarded ports per GPU (100 recommended). CGNAT and shared ISP IPs are not supported
SSH Access
SSH key authentication only. Password login enabled will fail verification
Updates
Update the kernel and all packages before running the installer
For the full list and the latest updates, see Minimum Requirements for Verification.

setup-storage.text:
Install Ubuntu Server and Storage Layout (~20 minutes)
Install the OS and plan your partitions ahead
Install Ubuntu Server
Download the 64-bit (AMD64) Ubuntu Server ISO and install it on your machine: https://releases.ubuntu.com/
- Ubuntu 24.04 is recommended for all GPUs.
- Ubuntu 22.04 should only be used if you have a specific need.
- Ubuntu 20.04 is end of life. Do not use it.
Note: We do not recommend the Desktop version. Please use the Server version only.
Storage Layout
Vast.ai software installs on the / mount point. Docker is installed on a separate mount point formatted with the XFS filesystem.
System and Vast.ai Software:
- EFI partition: at least 256 MB
- Root partition (ext4): at least 80 GB
The remaining disk space should be used for Docker. You may leave it as free space and configure it after OS installation.
Filesystem          Size    Type   Mounted on
──────────────────  ──────  ─────  ────────────────
/dev/sda1           256M+    -     /boot/efi
/dev/sda2           80G+    ext4   /              # VASTAI software will install here
/dev/sdb1           REST    xfs    /var/lib/docker # container data will be here
Option 1: Mount Docker to a Custom Partition (Recommended)
After OS installation, create a mount point and mount it to your largest partition or RAID array. No Docker install is needed at this stage.
Replace /dev/<partition> with your actual partition name:
Create XFS filesystem:
sudo mkfs.xfs -f /dev/<partition>
Get the UUID:
sudo blkid /dev/<partition>
Create mount point:
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/docker
Add fstab entry (replace <UUID> with the value from blkid output):
echo 'UUID=<UUID> /var/lib/docker xfs rw,auto,pquota 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
Mount it:
sudo mount /var/lib/docker
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
Confirm:
df -h
# /dev/<partition> 753G 15G 739G 2% /var/lib/docker
Option 2: Let the Installer Use the Largest Free Partition (Auto Select)
Leave the space unpartitioned (free space). The Vast.ai software installer will automatically detect the unpartitioned space, set up an XFS partition, and remount Docker.
Option 3: No Empty Partition (Auto Fallback)
If there is no empty partition or not enough free space, the installer will create a loopback (emulated) XFS partition as a fallback.
Note: A loopback device has lower performance than a dedicated partition. We recommend using an actual XFS partition whenever possible.

setup-driver.text:
Install NVIDIA GPU Driver & CUDA (~20 minutes)
The NVIDIA driver version you should install depends on your GPU model, so please choose a version that is compatible with your hardware. It's a good idea to review NVIDIA's compatibility notes before proceeding.
We recommend disabling Secure Boot before installing the driver.
Vast.ai works with NVIDIA drivers in general, but selecting the correct driver for your specific hardware is important, and some versions may be more stable than others.
Whenever possible, we recommend using the latest driver version, as it may improve performance and help attract renters. You can use any of the options listed below:
- Proprietary/open driver from Ubuntu drivers
- Open version from PPA
- Driver from the NVIDIA official site
Ultimately, whichever compatible driver works best for you is fine — we don't require a specific version. That said, using the latest CUDA-supported driver is recommended.
After installing, test your driver with nvidia-smi -q and other similar tests before proceeding.
Notes:
- If you are using SXM, don't forget to install related packages such as fabric manager.
- If you have Mellanox NICs, please configure them before installing the daemon.
- If you are using NVLink, make sure it can be seen by nvidia-smi.

setup-network.text:
Network Setup (~15 mins)
Port Requirements
- At least 5 open ports per GPU (100 open ports per GPU is recommended).
- The port range must be continuous, for both TCP and UDP, such as 16384-32768.
- The Vast software installer will prompt you for an open port range, so be prepared.
You can change the port range later by writing it to /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_port_range:
sudo bash -c 'echo -n "<START_PORT>-<END_PORT>" > /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_port_range'
Make sure there is no trailing newline.
You can still list a machine without open ports, but it is unlikely to get rentals and will not qualify for verification.
IP Requirements
- A dynamic IP is acceptable, but a static IP is preferred. The IP must be a public IPv4 address — CGNAT and shared ISP IPs are not supported.
- By default, your machine's public IP is the incoming IP that connects to our server.
For most networks this is sufficient, but sysadmins of unusual datacenter networks may want to override this behavior (useful for some asymmetric NATs/firewalls) by writing the IP to /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_ipaddr:
sudo bash -c 'echo -n "<YOUR_IP_ADDRESS>" > /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_ipaddr'
Note: If your machine's IP changes, you will need to restart the daemon:
sudo systemctl restart vastai
Speed Requirements
- Minimum: 10 Mbps upload/download per machine, but rentals are very unlikely at this speed.
- For verification: 500 Mbps upload/download per machine. Faster speeds are more appealing to clients.

setup-install.text:
Install the Vast.ai Manager Software (~15 minutes)
Use the copy button to copy and paste this command into a terminal. It will download the installer and run it with your unique authorization key.
The installer will install Docker, nvidia-ctk, and other related packages automatically.
Note: The installation command contains your account identity and is valid for one hour only. If it expires, refresh the page to generate a new command.
Note: If you get a 403 error, accept the hosting agreement again, refresh the page, and click the copy button. If you are on a team account, make sure you have machine read/write permissions.
Note: If you encounter driver problems, it is best to reinstall the NVIDIA driver first before running the Vast.ai installer.
Recommended for new hosts — guided TUI installer:
Please log in or sign up to get your authenticated install command.
Advanced users — standard installer:

setup-list.text:
List Your Machine (~5 minutes)
Go to the Machines page and find your new machine. It may take a few minutes to an hour for the main performance stats to appear. Ensure your machine is properly prepared to stay online and ready for long periods of continuous work.
If your machine doesn't appear, check vast_host_install.log, located in the directory where you ran the install script, for any errors. If there are no errors, refresh the page or try to run the installer again.
Click the Settings button. List your machine for rental using the List button, then adjust the max rental duration using the Availability date field. On the end date, the listing will expire and your machine will be unlisted. However, any existing client jobs will remain until ended by their owners.
Once your machine is listed and rented, it is extremely important that you do not interfere with it in any way. If your machine has an active client job and goes offline, crashes, or experiences performance problems, this could lower your reliability rating and trigger an SLA violation. We strongly recommend testing your machine first and only listing it when ready.
To read more about hosting: https://docs.vast.ai/host/hosting-overview

setup-test.text:
Test Your Machine (~10 minutes)
You can test your machine using our CLI. After downloading the Vast.ai CLI and setting up your API key, list your machine and ensure:
1. Your machine has been listed.
2. There are no active clients currently renting it.
Run the self-test command:
vastai self-test machine <machine_id>
Optional: Ignore Requirements Mode
If your machine is rejected for not meeting requirements but you still want to check its rentability or run the pressure tests, rerun the test with the --ignore-requirements flag:
vastai self-test machine <machine_id> --ignore-requirements
For full self-test documentation, see: How to Self-Test
Verification
When your machine is added to the platform, it will have the Unverified status. This just means that it has not yet had time to build up its reliability score and demonstrate that it can reliably sustain instances and stay connected to the platform. While it has this status, it is still searchable, but will not show up on the default search filters.
Machine verification is fully automated, and runs at least once each day. The system evaluates each machine using multiple criteria, including GPU model, demand, uptime, network stability, DLPerf, and overall reliability. There's no fixed timeline for verification. The best way to improve your chances is to ensure your machine passes all system tests, maintains high uptime, stable network connectivity, and strong DLPerf performance, and that it operates reliably over time.
Support is unable to expedite or manually influence this process. You can read more about how verification works here.

wizard-description.text:
**Vast.ai Host Installer Wizard** is a guided terminal front-end for listing a GPU machine as a host on the [Vast.ai](https://vast.ai) GPU cloud marketplace. It checks your hardware and walks you through networking, ports, and storage, then runs Vast.ai's official `install` script for you — it doesn't replace the installer, it makes running it guided and hard to get wrong.

It covers everything a host needs:

- **NVIDIA GPU drivers** and the **CUDA** runtime
- **Docker** with the **NVIDIA container runtime**, so rentals can use your GPUs
- The **Vast.ai host daemon** that lists your machine and manages rentals
- **Storage**, the host **port range**, and firewall reachability
- **Validation & registration** — NVML / NCCL self-tests, a speed test, and listing the machine

wizard-usage.text:
### Set up this machine as a Vast.ai host

1. Open **<https://cloud.vast.ai/host/setup/>** and download the **installer script** (it saves as a file named `install`). The page also shows an `install` command with your **API key** passed as an argument — copy the key out of that command.
2. Run the wizard as root, pointing it at that script and passing the key you copied:

```bash
sudo ./host-installer-wizard-linux-x86_64 \
    --installer-path ./install \
    --api-key <YOUR_API_KEY>
```

The wizard collects your inputs, then runs `install` to set up and register the machine. Root is required because the install changes system-level configuration.

### Command-line options

```
host-installer-wizard-linux-x86_64 [--installer-path PATH] [--api-key KEY] [--debug | --debug-live] [--start-at PAGE_ID]
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--installer-path PATH` | Path to the `install` script you downloaded from the host setup page. **Required for a real install;** ignored in `--debug`. |
| `--api-key KEY` | Your Vast.ai API key (the argument from the page's `install` command). Pre-fills the API-key step so you don't type it in the wizard. |
| `--debug` | **Simulation mode** — fake data, no real changes, `--installer-path` not needed. The safe way to preview the UI. |
| `--debug-live` | Real install with arrow-key page-skip enabled (advanced). Performs an actual install; mutually exclusive with `--debug`. |
| `--start-at PAGE_ID` | Jump straight to a page (e.g. `ports`, `storage`). Mainly a development aid. |

Run with no options to see the requirement check: the wizard exits and tells you `--installer-path` is required (or use `--debug`).

## What it does

Ten guided steps, each validating before you continue:

**Welcome → API key → NVIDIA/CUDA → System check → Network overview → Network speed → Ports → Storage → Review → Install + self-test.**

Each step runs real checks (GPU/VRAM, disk space, port reachability, upload/download speed, …) and explains what it found, so the machine is correctly configured *before* the install runs.

# shell command often appends '\n' or ' ' which would otherwise
        # produce a malformed Authorization header and a misleading 401.
        key = (self.app.state.api_key or "").strip()
        if not key:
            await self._show_invalid_ui()
            return
        try:
            timeout = aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=10)
            async with aiohttp.ClientSession(timeout=timeout) as session:
                async with session.get(
                    "https://console.vast.ai/api/v0/machines/",
                    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
                ) as resp:
                    if resp.status == 200:
                        # Validation can outlive the page (debug-mode arrow
                        # skip). Without this guard the NavigateNext would
                        # fire from whatever page is current, double-advancing.
                        if self.is_attached:
                            self.request_next()
                    else:
                        if resp.status == 403:
                            msg = (
                                "Registration failed. Please refresh the setup page and "
                                "copy the installation command again. "
                                "The installation key is only valid for one hour."
                            )
                        else:
                            try:
                                body = await resp.json(content_type=None)
                                server_msg = body.get("msg", "")
                                msg = f"{resp.status}: {server_msg}" if server_msg else f"{resp.status}"
                            except Exception:
                                msg = f"{resp.status}"
                        await self._show_invalid_ui(detail=msg, status=resp.status)

def preflight_requirement_checks(offer):
    gpu_total_ram = safe_float(offer.get("gpu_total_ram"))
    per_gpu_ram_gib = per_gpu_vram_gib(offer)
    required_mbps = required_inet_mbps(gpu_total_ram)
    cpu_ram = safe_float(offer.get("cpu_ram"))
    cpu_cores = int(safe_float(offer.get("cpu_cores")))
    num_gpus = int(safe_float(offer.get("num_gpus")))
    listed_gpus = num_gpus if num_gpus > 0 else 1
    direct_port_count = safe_float(offer.get("direct_port_count"))
    required_min_ports = 3 * listed_gpus
    recommended_max_ports = 64 * listed_gpus
    uncapped_required_cpu_ram = 0.95 * gpu_total_ram
    required_cpu_ram = min(uncapped_required_cpu_ram, SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB)
    required_cpu_cores = 2 * num_gpus

    checks = [
        _check(
            "cuda.version",
            "CUDA version",
            safe_float(offer.get("cuda_max_good")),
            11.8,
            ">=",
            "CUDA",
            safe_float(offer.get("cuda_max_good")) >= 11.8,
            "The self-test image needs a host driver stack compatible with CUDA 11.8 or newer.",
            "Update the NVIDIA driver/CUDA stack, then confirm with: vastai search offers "
            f"'machine_id={offer.get('machine_id') or 'unknown'} rentable=any rented=any'",
        ),
        _check(
            "reliability",
            "Reliability",
            safe_float(offer.get("reliability")),
            0.90,
            ">",
            "ratio",
            safe_float(offer.get("reliability")) > 0.90,
            "Self-test uses reliability as a guardrail before launching a temporary instance.",
            "Let the host stabilize and resolve recent failures before retrying the self-test.",
        ),
        _check(
            "network.direct_ports",
            "Direct port count",
            direct_port_count,
            required_min_ports,
            ">=",
            "ports",
            direct_port_count >= required_min_ports,
            (
                "The tester needs at least 3 directly mapped ports per listed GPU for remote "
                "progress, SSH checks, and runtime port allocation."
            ),
            (
                f"Open at least {required_min_ports} direct ports for {listed_gpus} listed GPU(s), "
                "check firewall/NAT forwarding, and make TCP/UDP forwarding symmetric where required."
            ),
        ),
        _check(
            "pcie.bandwidth",
            "PCIe bandwidth",
            safe_float(offer.get("pcie_bw")),
            2.85,
            ">",
            "GB/s",
            safe_float(offer.get("pcie_bw")) > 2.85,
            "Low PCIe bandwidth can make GPU stress and transfer checks fail or time out.",
            "Check BIOS PCIe generation/lane settings and confirm GPUs are seated in full-speed slots.",
        ),
        _check(
            "network.download",
            "Download speed",
            safe_float(offer.get("inet_down")),
            round(required_mbps, 2),
            ">=",
            "Mb/s",
            safe_float(offer.get("inet_down")) >= required_mbps,
            "The bandwidth floor scales with total VRAM so large GPU hosts can complete data movement tests.",

        ),

            ">=",
            "Mb/s",
            safe_float(offer.get("inet_up")) >= required_mbps,
            "The tester needs enough upload bandwidth to report progress and complete network checks.",
            "Improve host upload bandwidth or reduce contention, then rerun the Vast host verification.",
        ),
        _check(
            "gpu.ram",
            "GPU RAM",
            round(per_gpu_ram_gib, 2),
            7,
            ">",
            "GiB",
            per_gpu_ram_gib > 7,

        _check(

            ">=",
            "MiB",
            cpu_ram >= required_cpu_ram,
            (

            ),
            (
                "Add system RAM or reduce the listed GPU set so system RAM is at least 95% of "
                "total VRAM, up to the 2 TB cap."
            ),
        ),
        _check(
            "cpu.cores",
            "CPU cores",
            cpu_cores,
            required_cpu_cores,
            ">=",
            "cores",
            cpu_cores >= required_cpu_cores,
            "The tester expects at least two CPU cores per GPU for stable orchestration.",

            _info_check(

                "Direct port count advisory",
                direct_port_count,
                recommended_max_ports,

                ),
                (
                    "This is advisory only, not a self-test gate. Keep enough direct ports for "
                    "self-test and normal workloads, but avoid mapping very large unused ranges."
                ),
            )
        )
    return checks

    return [check for check in checks if check.get("status") == "fail"]


def informational_checks(checks):
    return [check for check in checks if check.get("status") == "info"]

    if not error:

    if isinstance(error, dict):

    response = getattr(error, "response", None)

    if isinstance(machine_lookup, dict) and "status" in machine_lookup:

        rows = machine_lookup.get("rows") or []
        if isinstance(rows, dict):

        return ("visible", [machine_lookup]) if machine_lookup else ("empty", [])

findmnt-definition.text: DESCRIPTION findmnt will list all mounted filesystems or search for a filesystem. The findmnt command is able to search in /etc/fstab , /etc/mtab or /proc/self/mountinfo . If device or mountpoint is not given, all filesystems are shown. The device may be specified by device name, major:minor numbers, filesystem label or UUID, or partition label or UUID. Note that findmnt follows mount (8) behavior where a device name may be interpreted as a mountpoint (and vice versa) if the --target , --mountpoint or --source options are not specified. The command-line option --target accepts any file or directory and then findmnt displays the filesystem for the given path.

findmnt-exit.text: EXIT STATUS The exit value is 0 if there is something to display, or 1 on any error (for example if no filesystem is found based on the user’s filter specification, or the device path or mountpoint does not exist).

docker-cgroup.text: Enumerate cgroups The file layout of cgroups is significantly different between v1 and v2. If /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers is present on your system, you are using v2, otherwise you are using v1. Refer to the subsection that corresponds to your cgroup version. cgroup v2 is used by default on the following distributions: Fedora (since 31) Debian GNU/Linux (since 11) Ubuntu (since 21.10) Important The detailed metrics examples later in this page describe the cgroup v1 file layout. On cgroup v2 hosts, use this page to find the container's cgroup directory and then inspect the controller files in that directory (for example, memory.* , cpu.* , and io.* ). For controller semantics, refer to the cgroup v2 kernel documentation . cgroup v1 You can look into /proc/cgroups to see the different control group subsystems known to the system, the hierarchy they belong to, and how many groups they contain. You can also look at /proc/<pid>/cgroup to see which control groups a process belongs to. The control group is shown as a path relative to the root of the hierarchy mountpoint. / means the process hasn't been assigned to a group, while /lxc/pumpkin indicates that the process is a member of a container named pumpkin . cgroup v2 On cgroup v2 hosts, the content of /proc/cgroups isn't meaningful. See /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers to the available controllers. Changing cgroup version Changing cgroup version requires rebooting the entire system. On systemd-based systems, cgroup v2 can be enabled by adding systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1 to the kernel command line. To revert the cgroup version to v1, you need to set systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0 instead. If grubby command is available on your system (e.g. on Fedora), the command line can be modified as follows: $ sudo grubby --update-kernel = ALL --args = "systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1" If grubby command isn't available, edit the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX line in /etc/default/grub and run sudo update-grub . Running Docker on cgroup v2 Docker supports cgroup v2 since Docker 20.10. Running Docker on cgroup v2 also requires the following conditions to be satisfied: containerd: v1.4 or later runc: v1.0.0-rc91 or later Kernel: v4.15 or later (v5.2 or later is recommended) Note that the cgroup v2 mode behaves slightly different from the cgroup v1 mode: The default cgroup driver ( dockerd --exec-opt native.cgroupdriver ) is systemd on v2, cgroupfs on v1. The default cgroup namespace mode ( docker run --cgroupns ) is private on v2, host on v1. The docker run flag --oom-kill-disable is discarded on v2.

hairpin.text:
6.  Hairpinning Behavior

   If two hosts (called X1 and X2) are behind the same NAT and
   exchanging traffic, the NAT may allocate an address on the outside of
   the NAT for X2, called X2':x2'.  If X1 sends traffic to X2':x2', it
   goes to the NAT, which must relay the traffic from X1 to X2.  This is
   referred to as hairpinning and is illustrated below.







Audet & Jennings         Best Current Practice                 [Page 16]
 
RFC 4787              NAT UDP Unicast Requirements          January 2007


     NAT
   +----+ from X1:x1 to X2':x2'   +-----+ X1':x1'
   | X1 |>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>--+---
   +----+                         |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
   +----+ from X1':x1' to X2:x2   |  v  | X2':x2'
   | X2 |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<--+---
   +----+                         +-----+

                           Hairpinning Behavior

   Hairpinning allows two endpoints on the internal side of the NAT to
   communicate even if they only use each other's external IP addresses
   and ports.

   More formally, a NAT that supports hairpinning forwards packets
   originating from an internal address, X1:x1, destined for an external
   address X2':x2' that has an active mapping to an internal address
   X2:x2, back to that internal address, X2:x2.  Note that typically X1'
   is the same as X2'.

   Furthermore, the NAT may present the hairpinned packet with either an
   internal (X1:x1) or an external (X1':x1') source IP address and port.
   Therefore, the hairpinning NAT behavior can be either "External
   source IP address and port" or "Internal source IP address and port".
   "Internal source IP address and port" may cause problems by confusing
   implementations that expect an external IP address and port.

   REQ-9:  A NAT MUST support "Hairpinning".

      a) A NAT Hairpinning behavior MUST be "External source IP address
         and port".

   Justification:  This requirement is to allow communications between
      two endpoints behind the same NAT when they are trying each
      other's external IP addresses.

      a) Using the external source IP address is necessary for
         applications with a restrictive policy of not accepting packets
         from IP addresses that differ from what is expected.
